en_summary: Google $GOOGL patent for 'My Channel' TV that generates personalized shows for an audience of one, casting user as lead with their look and voice, using viewing history for AI videos. Advertising already in design, stitching targeted ads. Things about to get crazy.
text:
🚨 This is one of the craziest things I’ve seen all year.

A newly public Google patent filing describes a TV channel that could generate shows for an audience of one. 

It could even cast you as the lead, with a character who looks like you and speaks in your voice. 

Google calls the concept “My Channel.” Open it and you’d see a lineup of titles and descriptions, much like any streaming app. 

The difference is where those titles come from. Google’s system would use your viewing history, language, location and age group to write prompts for AI to create videos specifically for you. 

Say you watch a lot of crime thrillers and comedies. 

Your channel could offer a crime comedy with you playing the detective. In one version of the design, the system would build your character from your photos and use a synthetic version of your voice to deliver the lines. 

The detail that caught my attention as a $GOOGL investor is that advertising is already in the design. 

The filing describes a system that could stitch targeted ads into the video before playback. Think about what that would mean for two people turning on their TVs at the same time. 

They could each get a different show, with a different lead character and a different advertiser. 

Things are about to get crazy.

zh_summary: 脫節。又一位凱恩斯主義者想加息50個基點。對現狀來說增長是壞事。Holtz-Eakin讀錯指標，聯準會不應跟隨。名義GDP不是過熱衡量。第三季名義6.2%，其中4.3為實際，價格1.9符合目標。
en_summary: Out of touch. Another Keynesian wanting 50 bps hike. Growth is bad to status quo. Holtz-Eakin reading wrong gauge, Fed shouldn’t follow. Nominal GDP not overheating measure. Q3 nominal 6.2% with 4.3 real, prices 1.9 consistent with target.
text:
Out of touch. Another Keynesian wanting 50 bps hike. 

To the status quo growth is bad. 

Holtz-Eakin is reading the wrong gauge, and the Fed shouldn’t follow him.

Nominal GDP is not a measure of overheating. It counts output and prices together. Third-quarter nominal growth was 6.2%, and 4.3 points of that was real output . Prices contributed about 1.9 points, which is target-consistent. Calling that “excessively demand-driven” misreads the arithmetic.

His argument also has no place for productivity. With GDP revised up, Q3 productivity is heading from 3.6% to 4.8% annualised. Hours barely moved, so the output is coming from each worker producing more. Unit labour costs were already falling, and that revision pushes them lower. Overheated demand does the opposite.

“Core inflation has never come close to 2%” is no case for a 50 basis point hike. The energy shock that has inflated prices will dissipate by spring, when the base effects roll off and PCE returns toward 2%. A hike cannot produce a barrel of oil. It would tighten against a price shock that is already ending, and a Fed that hikes to “send a message” is substituting posture for policy.

The cost of that message is large. A 50 basis point move would put the real funds rate above neutral and tighter than Greenspan’s in 1995, just as the productivity gains he bet on appear in the data. A Fed that cannot tell a supply boom from a demand boom should not set rates.

The economy is not overheating. It is getting more pro

text: The chip selling on yesterday had a specific cause, and it was not the tariff headline. The Commerce Department's November 16 rule closed the loophole that let Chinese firms rent Nvidia chips remotely through overseas data centers, and it took effect Nov 19. On Wednesday the consequence arrived in the open: sellers dumping Blackwell B300 GPUs on the secondary market, with servers quoted at $3M against a $600k list price, because the chips can no longer be rented to the customers they were bought for. TSMC has suspended previously permitted advanced chip orders from Chinese customers. The rule is aimed at the cloud loophole, and it works by cutting the rental route, not just the shipping route. For $NVDA the read is mixed: the demand is real, the chips are real, but a slice of that demand was Chinese money routed through Southeast Asia, and that slice is now stranded. The market is repricing which AI demand is durable and which was regulatory arbitrage.

Then the strange one: November CPI prints Dec 10, one day after the Fed decides, so the Fed hikes without seeing the inflation number it is hiking against. The payrolls number lands first, and a hot print there would harden the hike path before the Fed even meets. 

The following week brings $MU and $BB earnings on Dec 17, and the year closes with the JPM collar expiring Dec 31. Six dates, each one a verdict on the last. The market does not need all six to go right. It needs the first two not to go wrong.

text: The fear gauge told yesterday 's story better than the index did. The VIX spiked toward 35 in the morning as the tape flushed, then faded to around 28 by the close. The Nasdaq-100 is cheaper on forward earnings today than it was at the bottom of the dot-com crash.

Its forward P/E is  17x right now, the lowest in four years. At the October 2002 bottom, after the index had fallen 83%, the forward P/E was still 20-25x. The index stands 32 times higher than that bottom and cheaper on earnings.

The 2002 number needs its context. That ~20-25x sat on earnings that had collapsed, so it was never actually cheap. Today's ~17x sits on earnings that are real and still growing. Same multiple math, opposite setup.

zh_summary: 反彈至下跌的 200 日移動平均線是賣出而非買入的理由。200 日線是市場的長期趨勢線。當它下跌時，趨勢向下，反彈至該線是逆勢反彈，而非趨勢改變。
en_summary: A rally into a falling 200-day moving average is a reason to sell, not to buy. The 200-day is the market's long-term trend line. When it is falling, the trend is down, and a rally up to it is a bounce against the trend, not a change of trend.
text:
A rally into a falling 200-day moving average is a reason to sell, not to buy. Here is why, and it is worth knowing because we are living it right now.

The 200-day is the market's long-term trend line. When it is falling, the trend is down, and a rally up to it is a bounce against the trend, not a change of trend. Everyone who bought higher and is underwater waits for the rally back to the line to sell at a smaller loss, so supply piles up there. The first rally to a falling 200-day almost always gets rejected.

The fair question is: but at some point the rally will break through, so why sell? Because a real break has a signature. The line flattens first, price bases underneath it for weeks, then closes above it, holds above it, and comes back to retest it as support. Buying the rally into a falling line skips all of that. The right buy is the retest after the break is confirmed. You give up the first few points and your odds jump.

This is our tape today. $SPY closed $716.70 with its 200-day at $730.02 and still falling. Today's bounce never even got near the line. If Friday takes us above $730 and holds, the story changes, but the buy is the hold and the retest, not the rally into it.

en_summary: RealSimpleAriel emphasizes WHEN > WHERE, study daily chart and playbook for setups like support gap, 6/20, VWAP reclaim, ORB, prior high break.
text:
WHEN > WHERE

So many people want to fight for pennies on a big-picture trade idea.

When you take the time to study the daily chart and understand your playbook, whether you’re buying a support gap, a 6/20 setup, a VWAP reclaim, a 5-minute ORB or a break of the prior day’s high, these are relatively small nuances in the grand scheme of things.

Yes, I’m aware that certain entries allow for tighter risk management and potentially larger position sizes.

BUT, and this is the more important part, are you recognizing what is going on around you that would create the conditions necessary for your trade idea to actually work?

Over time, you’ll come to learn that WHEN you buy something is far more important than WHERE you bought it.

Show up to buy $SMH or $GLD after 10 a.m. today and you’re likely making money regardless of which entry technique you employed. But show up to buy those same names 2, 4 or 10 days ago, and you could have been getting destroyed because you failed to recognize that it wasn’t the proper “WHEN.”

You can have a textbook entry in the wrong environment and still lose money. Conversely, you can have a mediocre entry in the right environment and make a lot of money.

Spend more time studying the conditions that make your setups work and less time obsessing over the perfect entry.

Something to stew on over the holiday weekend. 🦃
